questions.stem: A 52-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. His symptoms developed 10 hours after a large meat feast. He had a history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation, controlled with bisoprolol. On admission, his temperature was 38.4°C, his blood pressure was 92/46 mmHg, and his heart rate was 126 beats/ min. He was markedly tender on abdominal exam. Investigations: Total white cell count 19.0 ×109/L Hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL Platelet count 100,000/μL Lactate 5 mmol/L Computed tomography scan of the abdomen showed possible ischemic and edematous dilated segments of bowel.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Clostridium perfringens Clostridial necrotizing enterocolitis (also known as pigbel disease in Papua New Guinea and “Darmbrand” in Germany) presents with segmental necrosis of the jejunum and ileum, severe abdominal pain, distension, and dilated loops of bowel. C. perfringens should be clinically suspected when a patient presents with a history of ingesting poorly cooked or stored meat or meat products (8–16 hours after). Both stool and food should be tested for toxin and cultured if possible and surgery to remove ischemic gut is required.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q19

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman developed flushing, blurring of vision, generalized itching, and perioral burning while eating at a restaurant. She had a salmon starter, followed by salad and swordfish, and had commented that her food was extremely spicy.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Scombroid poisoning Food poisoning associated with seafood is known as scombroid poisoning. It is commonly misdiagnosed as a seafood allergy. Poisoning is acquired through seafood consumption, especially dark meat of finfish from the Scombridae and Scomberesocidae families, such as tuna, mackerel, skipjack, and bonito; other fish such as dolphin fish, tilapia, salmon, swordfish, trout, sardines, and anchovies have been implicated. Symptoms are due to histamine reaction occurring within 1 hour of consumption. Fish may appear to have “honey-combed” scales and taste “peppery,” “bubbly,” or “spicy.” Elderly patients and those taking medication which prevent the breakdown of histamine such as monoamine oxidase inhibitors or isoniazid are likely to have more severe and prolonged symptoms as compared with those taking antihistamines.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q18

questions.stem: A 43-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of hallucinations, vertigo, and paraesthesia. He had also had a 24-hour period of diarrhea which had resolved. His symptoms started 5 hours after he had been to a local seafood restaurant. He could not recall anything unusual about his meal, which had tasted fine.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.explanation: Ciguatera poisoning Fish with ciguatera toxin do not look, smell, or taste any different, unlike with scombroid poisoning. Caribbean ciguatera poisoning is not life-threatening and presents with gastrointestinal symptoms followed by neurologic signs without altered mental status. Neurologic signs (weakness, paresthesia, headache, vertigo, pruritus, hallucinations) develop within 3–72 hours after consumption, with abnormalities persisting for several weeks to months (20%). Ciguatera poisoning should be notified to the local health protection unit and regional poison center to identify the source and affected reef.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q9

questions.stem: Three people are brought to the emergency department by ambulance from a conference at a hotel banquet hall. All had been taken ill within a short time of eating at a buffet that included fresh tuna. The patients all complained of headache, dizziness, and flushing. They were all mildly tachycardic, but none was febrile or hypotensive.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of their symptoms?
questions.explanation: Histamine ingestion These patients have scombroid poisoning, which is caused by excess histamine production from bacterial overgrowth in poorly cleaned or stored fish. It is most commonly seen with oily fish, including tuna and mackerel. Symptoms include flushing, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness, and palpitations, and patients typically become symptomatic within an hour of ingesting the contaminated seafood.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q40

questions.stem: About 8 hours after eating a seafood dinner, a patient develops diarrhea, bradycardia, temperature-related dysesthesia and circumoral paresthesiae.
questions.lead_in: Her symptoms are most suggestive of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Ciguatera poisoning She most likely has ciguatoxin poisoning. Early symptoms can include abdominal cramps, diarrhea and circumoral paresthesiae. Later neurologic symptoms can include a sensation of reversal of hot and cold perception.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q39

questions.stem: An outbreak of illness was reported among 50 people eating at a local restaurant. These individuals had an illness that consisted of predominately vomiting but nausea, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea were also present. Fever was present in the majority of the affected individuals. The median incubation period was 31 hours. The illness lasted approximately 48 hours. Only one person required hospitalization.
questions.lead_in: What was the most likely cause of the outbreak?
questions.explanation: Norovirus The illness fits criteria for a norovirus outbreak. Vomiting predominated, the incubation period was between 24 and 48 hours, and the illness lasted between 12 and 60 hours. This is not STEC because if STEC was the cause of such an outbreak, hospitalization and hemolytic–uremic syndrome would have been seen. Bloody diarrhea was not mentioned in the stem. Vomiting would not have predominated for infection due to Campylobacter, and the illness would have lasted longer. ETEC typically causes more of a watery diarrhea but not prominent vomiting. The incubation period is too long for staphylococcal food poisoning, which is between 2 and 7 hours.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q27

questions.question: An outbreak of Escherichia coli O157:H7 occurs in a nursing home; an epidemic curve is provided.
questions.question_raw: Outbreak question about E.coli 0157:H7 with epi curve

parts.text: Provide: 2 resident interventions; 2 staff interventions; 2 environmental interventions; 1 quality assurance intervention; type of curve; attack rate; incubation period; host/pathogen factors influencing spread

parts_raw.text: Provide: 2 resident interventions; 2 staff interventions; 2 environmental interventions; 1 quality assurance intervention; type of curve; attack rate; incubation period; host/pathogen factors influencing spread

questions.model_answer:
a) Residents (2): (1) Contact precautions with single room or cohorting of symptomatic/incontinent residents, dedicated equipment, and exclusion from communal dining and recreational water until resolved; (2) Supervised hand hygiene for residents and counselling to avoid swimming, water activities, and sexual contact while symptomatic.
Staff (2): (1) Reinforced hand hygiene and gloves/gowns for care of symptomatic residents, with strict separation of food-handling from direct care duties; (2) Active identification of ill staff with exclusion of symptomatic staff and food handlers from work until transmission risk is sufficiently reduced per public health criteria.
Environmental (2): (1) Enhanced cleaning/disinfection of washrooms, commodes and high-touch surfaces, with dedicated or disposable equipment; (2) Review of the food service: remove and hold suspect food, correct cooking/holding temperatures, prevent cross-contamination via cutting boards and utensils, and stop any unpasteurized milk or juice.
Quality assurance (1): Formal outbreak investigation — line list and case definition, stool cultures/CIDT with isolates sent for PFGE/WGS subtyping (PulseNet), notification to public health, and audit of hand hygiene and food-handling practice with feedback.
Type of curve: propagated (person-to-person) spread following the initial common-source exposure, indicated by successive case peaks about one incubation period apart across all four units.
Attack rate: number of cases divided by number of residents at risk x 100 (cannot be computed without the denominator on the curve).
Incubation period: about 3 to 4 days (range 1 to 10 days).
Host/pathogen factors: pathogen — very low infectious dose, Shiga toxin 1/2 production (Stx2 strains more virulent) and adherence factors, prolonged faecal shedding; host — advanced age and comorbidity with higher HUS/case fatality (33% in adults 60 years and older), incontinence and cognitive impairment limiting hygiene, gastric acid suppression, and shared communal space/staff.
questions.beyond_mandell: PHAC/CDC enteric outbreak guidance: incubation 3-4 days (range 1-10) and exclusion of cases from food handling/direct care until asymptomatic (often 2 negative stools) are not stated in this chapter.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort calls the curve simply propagated; the chapter's framing supports a common-source outbreak with subsequent propagated person-to-person spread, which is what involvement of all four units implies.

cohort_answer.text: Resident: isolation of those with symptoms; handwashing. Staff: increased hand washing; using proper PPE. Environmental: single person bathrooms; disinfection of rooms. QA: investigation/tracking of cases. Type of curve: propagated. Attack rate/incubation period: can't calculate without the curve. Host/pathogen factors: host susceptibility; basic reproductive number/infectivity.

questions.question: A group develops food poisoning about 4 hours after a meal.

parts.text: What is the mechanism and what are the organisms responsible?

parts_raw.text: What is the mechanism and what are the organisms responsible?

questions.model_answer: a) Mechanism: ingestion of a preformed, heat-stable enterotoxin already present in the food (not infection), producing vomiting-predominant illness with a short incubation of 1 to 8 hours and duration under 24 hours. Organisms: (1) Staphylococcus aureus (staphylococcal enterotoxins SEA-SEV, SEA most common; heat- and protease-resistant, emesis via vagal stimulation); (2) Bacillus cereus, emetic syndrome (cereulide, incubation 0.5-6 hours).

cohort_answer.text: S. aureus – potent enterotoxin (SEA, SEB, SEC etc) that triggers upper GI syndrome (primarily vomiting). B. cereus – similar emetic toxin and 5 enterotoxins. Typically toxin-mediated food poisoning has an incubation of 1-6h, less than 12h

questions.question: On an Alaskan cruise ship, four patients complain of nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain.
questions.question_raw: Alaskan cruise-ship with 4 patients c/o N/V and abdominal pain.

parts.text: Name 3 toxin-mediated syndromes that can cause this picture
What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?

parts_raw.text: Name 3 toxin-mediated syndromes that can cause this picture
What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Staphylococcus aureus preformed enterotoxin food poisoning (incubation 1-8 hours, vomiting predominant, under 24 hours); (2) Bacillus cereus emetic syndrome from cereulide (0.5-6 hours), or its diarrheal toxin syndrome (8-16 hours); (3) Clostridium perfringens type A enterotoxin (CPE) illness, incubation 9-12 hours, cramps and diarrhea with little vomiting.
b) Norovirus gastroenteritis — the classic cruise ship outbreak agent, spread by food handlers, contaminated food or water, and person-to-person/fomite, with acute vomiting, cramps and short self-limited illness (median incubation about 1 day).

cohort_answer.text: Toxin-mediated syndromes: S. aureus; C. perfringens; B. cereus; (also consider V. cholerae, C. difficile). Most likely diagnosis: Norovirus.

questions.question: A group of patients develop nausea, vomiting and diaphoresis approximately 3 hours (range 1-7 hours) after eating ham.
questions.question_raw: Group of patients develop nausea/vomiting/diaphoresis approximately 3 hrs (range 1-7) after eating ham.

parts.text: What are the most likely organisms and syndrome?
How do you test for it?

parts_raw.text: What are the most likely organisms and syndrome?
How do you test for it?

questions.model_answer:
a) Syndrome: preformed enterotoxin food poisoning causing nausea and vomiting lasting under 24 hours (incubation 1-8 hours). Organisms: Staphylococcus aureus (SEA-SEV enterotoxins; ham, poultry, salads and sandwiches are the classic vehicles, usually contaminated by a food handler and then held at improper temperature) and, less likely with ham, emetic Bacillus cereus (cereulide).
b) Diagnosis is clinical. Outbreak confirmation: isolate S. aureus of the same subtype from vomitus or stool of two or more ill people, or from both patient and food; or detect enterotoxin (reverse passive latex agglutination or ELISA for SEA-SEE, or mass spectrometry) or greater than 10^5 organisms per gram in the implicated food; note the organism is heat-labile and often not recoverable from cooked food although toxin persists. Send leftover food to a food microbiology laboratory and collect stool from multiple patients to exclude other causes.

cohort_answer.text: S. aureus (SEA-SEV toxins) or B. cereus - preformed enterotoxin-mediated; short incubation 1-8h, illness generally self-limiting <24h. Testing: Clinical diagnosis; can do stool cultures to rule out other causes; blood cultures if unstable.

questions.question: An outbreak of Escherichia coli O157:H7 in a nursing home is presented with an epidemic curve; the residence has 4 units and all are affected.
questions.question_raw: Outbreak question about E.coli 0157:H7 with epi curve. States that residence has 4 units, and all are affected.

parts.text: What kind of outbreak is this, based on the curve?
Name 1 pathogen factor and 1 host factor that are related to the type of outbreak
2 infection control measures pertaining to residents, 2 infection control measures pertaining to nursing home staff

parts_raw.text: A. What kind of outbreak is this, based on the curve?
B. Name 1 pathogen factor and 1 host factor that are related to the type of outbreak:
C. 2 infection control measures pertaining to residents, 2 infection control measures pertaining to nursing home staff:
D. What is the incubation period?

questions.model_answer:
a) A propagated (person-to-person) outbreak — multiple successive peaks about one incubation period apart with involvement of all four units, following an initial common-source (food) exposure.
b) Pathogen factor: very low infectious dose with prolonged faecal shedding, allowing efficient secondary faecal-oral transmission. Host factor: elderly, often incontinent or cognitively impaired residents who cannot perform hand hygiene and who share communal space and caregivers (and who have higher rates of HUS and death).
c) Residents (2): (1) Contact precautions — single room or cohorting of symptomatic/incontinent residents with dedicated equipment; (2) Exclusion from communal dining, group activities and recreational water plus assisted hand hygiene until symptoms resolve.
Staff (2): (1) Reinforced hand hygiene and gloves/gowns for all contact with symptomatic residents, with staff cohorted to affected units and not performing food handling; (2) Active surveillance for ill staff and exclusion of symptomatic staff and food handlers from work until the transmission risk is sufficiently reduced.
d) About 3 to 4 days (range 1 to 10 days).
questions.beyond_mandell: PHAC/CDC: the 3-4 day (1-10 day) STEC incubation and the staff exclusion criteria (asymptomatic, often 2 negative stools) come from public health guidance, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text:
Common Source Outbreak; Person-to-person outbreak (index case with limited spread -> quickly controlled); Propagated spread -> ongoing secondary spread. [reviewed 2014 exam - looks like propagated spread from point source/index]
Pathogen: Incubation period; Infecting dose (very small here); R0. Host: secondary attack rate; Immune status – can affect period of communicability aka duration of time organism excreted, usually 1 week or less in adults; mode of transmission aka fecal oral
Staff: Hand hygiene to be emphasized; Use contact precautions for incontinent or diapered residents afflicted; Food handling measures; Identify new staff cases and exclude them from work; Exclusion criteria (2 negative stool specimens 24h apart etc). Residents: Dedicated equipment if reusable, dedicated nurses; Cohorting or single patient rooms if possible and incontinent; Avoid communal spaces, pools/hot tubs until 48 hours after symptom resolution
2-10 days, median 3-4

questions.question: On an Alaskan cruise ship, four patients complain of nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain.
questions.question_raw: Q11 (2007). Alaskan cruise-ship with 4 patients c/o n/v and abd pain

parts.text: Name 3 toxin-mediated syndromes that can cause this picture?
What is the most likely diagnosis?

parts_raw.text: A) Name 3 toxin-mediated syndromes that can cause this picture?
B) What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning — preformed, heat-resistant enterotoxins (SEA-SEV), incubation 1-8 hours, vomiting 87%, diarrhea 89%, fever uncommon, resolves under 24 hours; (2) Bacillus cereus — two syndromes: short-incubation emetic (cereulide, 0.5-6 hours) and long-incubation diarrheal (8-16 hours); (3) Clostridium perfringens type A — enterotoxin CPE, incubation 9-12 hours, cramps and watery diarrhea with minimal vomiting.
b) Norovirus gastroenteritis (not toxin-mediated): the leading foodborne and cruise ship outbreak agent, acute vomiting with cramps, median incubation about 1 day, illness 1-3 days, spread by contaminated food/water, food handlers, and person-to-person or fomite contact.

cohort_answer.text: A) Staphylococcus aureus (preformed toxin, heat resistant enterotoxins); C. perfringens (toxin A, diarrhea, abd pain, minimal vomiting); B. cereus (preformed toxin, 2 syndromes - short incubation emetic 0.5-6h and long incubation diarrheal 8-16h). B) Norovirus gastroenteritis (not toxin-mediated).

questions.question: A man on vacation in the tropics eats copious seafood and develops abdominal malaise, heat flashes and perioral paresthesia, worse with alcohol, for the last several weeks.
questions.question_raw: Q12 (2007). Man on vacation in the tropics. Copious seafood consumption. Develops abdominal malaise, heat flashes, and peri-oral parasthesia. Worse with ETOH, all for the last several weeks.

parts.text: Counsel regarding the natural history of this condition

parts_raw.text: D) Counsel regarding the natural history of this condition

questions.model_answer:
a) Ciguatera fish poisoning (ciguatoxin, a heat-stable lipid-soluble dinoflagellate toxin that opens voltage-sensitive sodium channels).
b) Large carnivorous reef fish from tropical coastal waters in which the toxin bioaccumulates: barracuda, amberjack, grouper and red snapper.
c) Supportive: rehydration, analgesia for dysesthesias, ventilatory support if respiratory failure; enemas or cathartics to remove unabsorbed toxin if there is no ileus; no antitoxin exists. Intravenous mannitol has been suggested by case reports and unblinded studies but a double-blind randomized trial showed no benefit. Amitriptyline or tocainide may help persistent dysesthesias.
d) Illness begins 6-24 hours after the meal with gastrointestinal, cardiovascular and neurologic features (perioral and extremity paresthesias, hot/cold temperature reversal, metallic taste, bradycardia, hypotension). The gastrointestinal and cardiovascular symptoms resolve within a few days, but neurologic symptoms may persist for weeks to years; the toxin is heat stable so cooking does not prevent it, and symptoms can recur with re-exposure — advise avoiding large reef fish, and alcohol, which precipitated his symptoms.
questions.beyond_mandell: Recurrence triggers (alcohol, caffeine, nuts, fish, exertion) and the advice to avoid them for months are conventional teaching rather than explicit in this chapter.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort recommends single-dose mannitol; the chapter notes a double-blind randomized trial found no benefit, so mannitol should not be considered standard therapy.

cohort_answer.text: A) Ciguatera fish poisoning. B) Large predatory reef fish: Moray eel, Amberjack, Barracuda, Red snapper, Grouper fish. C) Supportive - manage dehydration, pruritis (antihistamines), hemodynamic instability (atropine for bradycardia); consider single dose mannitol once volume repleted; don't use antimotility agents. D) Symptoms begin within hours up to 30h (GI) and 72h (neurologic); GI/CV signs resolve by 24-48h, rarely persist beyond 4 days; neurological abnormalities may persist weeks; ETOH, caffeine, nuts, fish, and excessive exertion can exacerbate/cause recurrence, avoid 6 months after initial episode; avoid sex until symptoms resolve or use condoms.
